questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what a reader can check when judging a narrator's reliability
questions.stem: A narrator is a source telling a reader what happened, not a record of it. What does that mean for judging whether the narrator can be trusted?

options.text: Whether what the narrator reports stays consistent with what the text shows elsewhere, since a teller can be compared and a record cannot
Whether the narrator tells the story in the first person, since the first person has access to the inside of events
options.misconception: treats grammatical person as a measure of accuracy, which confuses access to a mind with truth about events

options.text: Whether the narrator is sympathetic, since a teller we like is more likely to be telling it straight
options.misconception: judges accuracy by likability, which is a preference and not a check on anything reported

options.text: Whether the narrator knows every character's thoughts, since total knowledge removes the possibility of error
options.misconception: assumes knowledge removes error, when a narrator who knows everything can still report wrongly

questions.explanation: Reliability is a question about a narrator's reporting, and it becomes answerable only when something else in the text can be set against it. A narrator may be wrong about a motive, mistaken about a date, or evasive about a fact, and in each case the evidence is the same: something the text reports elsewhere, or something the narrator reports inconsistently. That is why a reader can say a narrator is unreliable when the text contradicts itself. The second option confuses having access to a mind with reporting events accurately, which are separate capacities. The third judges truth by likability, which no reading method supports. The fourth mistakes information for accuracy, and an omniscient narrator can be as wrong as any other.
questions.hint: Ask what the text reports that the narrator's account would have to agree with.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: identify the sentence in which a narrator's unreliability is visible
questions.stem: An invented narrator writes: "I was the only one in the room who heard the bell, and I will say again that I was the only one, and that the others looked at me and said nothing, which is what they always do when they cannot face a fact." Which sentence is the evidence for calling this narration unreliable?

options.text: The last clause, since it turns the narrator's own difficulty into a habit of the other people and so puts the ground under his own account
The word again, since a narrator who has told the bell story twice has a habit and an account at once
options.misconception: treats repetition as proof of falsity, though people truthfully repeat what they have already said

options.text: The claim to have been the only one, since the passage reports no other witness and so he cannot know he was alone
options.misconception: argues from the text's silence to the narrator's error, which may only be the narrator's silence

options.text: The whole passage, since it names a bell and a room and no one else, and a scene that thin cannot support an account
options.misconception: rejects the whole report as thin, which confuses a narrow report with a false one

questions.explanation: The tell is the last clause, because it is where the narration does something a report does not: it explains other people. The other men looked at him and said nothing, which may be true, and then the narrator supplies the reason, which is that they always do this when they cannot face a fact. That reason is available to him and to nobody else, and attaching it to them is how the account defends itself against the possibility that he is the one who cannot face it. The second option treats a repeated claim as evidence of falsity, which is not how repetition works. The third argues from what the passage has left out, and a narrator's silence is not a contradiction. The fourth dismisses the whole report for narrowness, which is a complaint about scope rather than about truth.
questions.hint: Ask which clause supplies a motive the narrator could not possibly know.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what free indirect discourse borrows from the narrator and from the character
questions.stem: A novel renders a character's thought in the narrator's own grammar and tense, with no quotation marks and no tag such as she thought. What is the arrangement called, and what does it do?

options.text: Free indirect discourse, and it lets a sentence belong to both voices at once, so a character's judgment arrives already inside the narration's movement
Free indirect discourse, and it changes nothing in either voice, since the thought is simply translated into the narrator's words
options.misconception: keeps the term and denies the two-voice effect, which is the whole point of the arrangement

options.text: Reported speech, since a character's silent thinking must be given in the narrator's language to be heard at all
options.misconception: confuses the unmarked rendering with quoted interior speech, which announces its own quotation

options.text: Stream of consciousness, since the passage is a mind reported without any of the narrator's apparatus around it
options.misconception: reaches for a broader term and loses the specific arrangement of grammar and tense

questions.explanation: The arrangement is free indirect discourse, and the two things it borrows are the narrator's grammar and the character's content. A sentence like it was obvious he would not come runs in the narration's tense and syntax and no quotation marks, so it is grammatically the narrator's, and yet the obvious is a judgment nobody but the character would make, so it is semantically hers. The reader is therefore given a thought from inside the narration rather than in a separate block, and a character's bias reaches the page without a tag announcing that it is bias. The second option keeps the name and deletes the effect, which makes the device pointless. The third confuses it with quoted speech, which marks its own boundaries. The fourth is a broader name for a family of effects and does not identify this one.
questions.hint: Ask whose grammar a sentence uses and whose judgment it carries.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Free indirect discourse identified in a passage
questions.learningObjective: locate free indirect discourse in a passage and say what it adds
questions.stem: A passage runs: "The coach was late again. He had said it would be late, and he had been right about that, which was not a comfort. Two hours on the end of a platform is a long time to think about nothing, and he thought about his mother, and then he stopped, and then he began again." Which part is free indirect discourse, and what does it do?

options.text: The sentences carrying which was not a comfort and and he thought about his mother, since both put the character's judgment inside the narration's own syntax with no tag to claim them
Only He had said it would be late, since the past perfect belongs to the narration and shared tense must mean shared voice
options.misconception: matches tense to the narration and calls a shared tense proof that a sentence is not interior

options.text: Only the last sentence, since the repetition of and then marks a mind losing its thread rather than reporting one
options.misconception: reads a repeated connective as psychological evidence, which is a guess about a person and not a reading of the syntax

options.text: None of the sentences, since the passage stays outside every character and reports only what a bystander could see
options.misconception: denies the passage any interior content, which its reported thinking plainly supplies

questions.explanation: Both of those sentences are grammatically the narration's and evidentially the character's, which is the definition of the arrangement. Which was not a comfort is a judgment no narrator would volunteer in that syntax, and he thought about his mother reports the content of a thinking in the third person the narration has been using, with no tag and no quotation marks. The effect is that a character's bias is delivered as narration, so the reader receives it without being told to distrust it. The second option is the diagnostic error: a shared tense is a consequence of the technique, not a refutation of it. The third reads syntax as symptom. The fourth denies the passage the interior it plainly reports.
questions.hint: Ask which sentences are grammatically narration but evidentially someone's judgment.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what a shift in focalisation changes in a scene
questions.stem: Focalisation is the question of whose limited knowledge a narration reports. What does a shift in it change?

options.text: What the reader is entitled to know inside the scene, so a fact the text has been withholding can be given without the events moving at all
The person the narration speaks in, so the passage moves from third person to first and back again
options.misconception: confuses a change of grammatical person with a change of whose knowledge governs the scene

options.text: The place the scene occupies, so the setting changes and the narration's viewpoint travels with it
options.misconception: attaches focalisation to location, when the limit is on what can be known and not on where it happens

options.text: The tense the narration reports in, so a story moves from what happened to what is being remembered
options.misconception: reads a tense change as a limit on knowledge, which are separate decisions a novelist makes

questions.explanation: Focalisation is a limit on knowledge, not a feature of grammar or geography, and a shift in it is therefore a change in what a scene can show. If a chapter has been locked to one character and then a paragraph moves to another, the reader loses the assurance that everything the scene reported went through the first character's senses, and gains whatever the second one perceives. That is a redistribution of knowledge with no change of event, and it is the device that lets a text reveal something while keeping its chronology intact. The second option confuses the grammatical person with the limit on knowledge, which can move while the pronoun stays the same. The third and fourth each attach focalisation to a feature that may stay exactly the same while it moves.
questions.hint: Ask whose senses everything in the scene has had to pass through.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: identify whose knowledge limits a passage and where the limit falls
questions.stem: A passage runs: "Maren watched the ferry come in and counted the people on it, three times, and got the same number. Osric had gone down to the slip to meet his brother, and had been gone an hour, and the light on the water had not told her anything at all." Whose knowledge limits this passage, and from where?

options.text: Maren's, and the whole passage is inside her attention, since the counting and the report about the light are things only she is doing or noticing
Osric's, since the passage's second sentence reports where he has been and for how long
options.misconception: picks the focaliser by who is the subject of information, when the limit follows whose senses are described

options.text: Nobody's, since the passage reports events in the past tense and the past tense is a claim of total knowledge
options.misconception: treats a tense as a claim about how much is known, which it makes on its own

options.text: Both at once, since a passage that names two people cannot be limited to either of them
options.misconception: assumes naming two people defeats a limit on knowledge, which is set by attention and not by who is mentioned

questions.explanation: The test is not who the passage talks about but who is doing the perceiving, and here every verb of perception belongs to Maren: she watched, she counted, three times, and the light had not told her anything. Osric's movements are available to her as things she knows, which is the ordinary condition of a limited narration, and the final pronoun closes the passage inside her. The second option is the commonest error, because the sentence about Osric looks like a change of vantage, but knowing where someone has been is not the same as seeing it. The third confuses a tense with a claim about knowledge. The fourth assumes a passage cannot be about two people and inside one mind, which is the normal condition of a novel.
questions.hint: Ask which sentences report something perceived and which report something known.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a description of a place carry emotion
questions.stem: A novelist describes the same hallway in every chapter, always as a clock, a radiator, a notice about lost property, and four chairs. What would make that description carry emotional weight rather than function as a backdrop?

options.text: The characters being unable to stop noticing those four things, so the description reports their state as much as the hallway's
The description growing longer as the book goes on, so that more of the hallway is available to carry feeling
options.misconception: equates the amount of description with its load, which is a measure of detail and not of effect

options.text: The hallway staying identical in every chapter, which is what lets a reader measure change against a fixed thing
options.misconception: makes constancy the source of the weight, when a setting earns weight by being read differently each time

options.text: The description coming last in each chapter, which lets it summarise the events that came before
options.misconception: reduces the effect to a position on the page, which any closing paragraph could claim

questions.explanation: A setting carries weight when the description is a record of attention rather than an inventory of the place, and attention is the reader's clearest route into a character's state. Four chairs and a radiator are neutral; four chairs and a radiator that a character counts while waiting, or cannot stop looking at while deciding something, are a report of that character, and the same objects will then be read differently in each chapter. The second option mistakes length for load, and a longer description of a place can be more indifferent than a short one. The third is half right and half wrong, because a fixed setting does give a reader something to measure against, but the weight comes from the changing reading rather than from the sameness. The fourth is about position, which is not what makes a description mean anything.
questions.hint: Ask whose attention the description is really recording.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: choose between two descriptions by what the observer's activity makes the objects do
questions.stem: One chapter inventories a house: hall, stairs, kitchen, two cupboards, a garden. A later chapter of an invented novel inventories the same house while the observer is packing: "two cups and one saucer, the saucer in the sink, a chair pushed back from the table, and the second cup in the box with the papers." Which account better supports the claim that the second chapter's setting carries emotional weight?

options.text: The second, since its objects are fixed while what the observer is doing makes each of them an item in an inventory of leaving
The first, since a complete inventory gives a reader more of the place to feel about than a partial one does
options.misconception: prefers completeness of description, when the question is what the objects are being made to mean

options.text: The second, since an observer who is packing is necessarily an unreliable one and so the place cannot be straightforward
options.misconception: infers unreliability from activity, which is a separate question from what a setting does

options.text: Neither, since a setting carries weight only when the objects in it have actually changed by the end
options.misconception: requires the objects themselves to alter, ignoring that a fixed object read differently does the work

questions.explanation: The two chapters describe the same house and the second is the one carrying the weight, and the difference is not in the house but in what the observer is doing to it. Every object in the second chapter is a thing that will be left, counted or not: the second cup is in the box, the saucer is in the sink, the chair has been pushed back and left that way. The first chapter's list is the same house described as a place to live in, and it stays that way under any reading. The second option prefers the more complete inventory, which measures detail rather than meaning. The third is a non sequitur, since packing is not a fact about a narrator's accuracy. The fourth sets a condition the chapters do not meet and do not need to, since nothing in the house has changed by the end of either chapter.
questions.hint: Ask what the observer is doing to the objects, and what that makes them.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what it means to put a narrative's conflict in the form of a question
questions.stem: A story's central conflict can be stated as a question the text is built to raise. What does that framing let a reader do?

options.text: Test whatever answer the text supplies against the text's own doings, since a question the book raises can be judged by whether the book answers it
Know whose side to take at once, since a stated conflict is a disagreement somebody has already announced
options.misconception: reduces a conflict to an announced disagreement, and so excludes conflicts no character ever voices

options.text: Name the obstacle that stands between the characters and what they want, which is what a question is naming
options.misconception: defines conflict narrowly as an obstacle, leaving out conflicts of belief and loyalty

options.text: Predict the ending, since a question the book raises is a question the book has already decided how to answer
options.misconception: assumes the question is settled in the text's first paragraphs, which would make the rest redundant

questions.explanation: Framing a conflict as a question makes the text answerable, which is the advantage of the framing. A reader can hold the question in mind while the text proceeds and then ask of the ending whether it has in fact answered the thing that was asked, and that is a test the text cannot avoid by being moving. It also explains why a novel may raise a question it never settles and still be complete: the question is a real object of the book even when the answer is refused. The second option narrows conflict to a disagreement a character announces aloud, which excludes most conflicts in most novels. The third defines conflict as an obstacle, which is one kind. The fourth assumes a question is settled early, and a question settled early is not worth raising.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would hold in mind while reading to the end.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: identify the question an invented text raises and how it is treated
questions.stem: An invented text runs: "The house had been empty for two years. A man came in October to measure it, for a sale that did not happen. He counted the rooms and wrote the numbers on his hand, and went out again, and left the key in the door, and that is the whole of what is recorded." What question does this text raise, and how does it treat it?

options.text: Why the sale did not happen, and the text leaves it open, since the key in the door is the only thing it offers and it never explains the act
No question at all, since a text that records only what is recorded has had nothing to raise
options.misconception: assumes an unstated cause cannot be a question, when an unexplained act is the ordinary source of one

options.text: What the key means, and the text answers it, since leaving a key in a door is presented as a deliberate act
options.misconception: takes the narrator's conjunction as a verdict on motive, when it only joins two observations

options.text: Who owned the house, and the text answers it, since it calls the visitor a man and no one else
options.misconception: treats a single word about a visitor as an answer to a question about ownership

questions.explanation: A text raises a question wherever it places an event it does not account for, and this one places two of them: a sale that did not happen, and a key left in a door. The question the reader is left with is why, and the text's only evidence is that the man left the key, which could be carelessness, a plan, a message, or an intention to come back, and the closing clause claims a completeness that makes the silence deliberate rather than an omission. That is what leaves the question open while keeping it a real object. The second option assumes a question has to be stated, and the closing clause is precisely the statement that it need not be. The third and fourth both read a narrator's connecting word as an explanation of motive, which is not what a conjunction does.
questions.hint: Ask which two events the text places and then does not account for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a narrative's action rise
questions.stem: A novel's middle stretch is called rising action. What is rising in it?

options.text: The character's situation, which loses an option at a time, so that by the end there is one course left rather than several
The pace, since a quickening of events is what tells a reader that the tension is building
options.misconception: identifies the rise with speed, which can stay slow while the situation narrows

options.text: The number of people in the scene, since a crowded room necessarily leaves a character less room to act
options.misconception: assumes more people means less room, and ignores a character who gains allies

options.text: The amount the narration tells the reader, since a reader's growing information marks the rise
options.misconception: locates the rise in what the reader is told rather than in what the character can do

questions.explanation: Action rises when the character's available courses decrease, and that is what a reader experiences as acceleration. If a character begins a stretch with four things she might do and ends it with one, no scene needs to be more dramatic than the one before for the reader to feel the pressure increasing, because what is increasing is the cost of the remaining options. That is also why rising action can be slow in tempo and still be unmistakable. The second option is the popular identification and it is a different thing: pace is a fact about sentences and scenes, and it can rise while the situation is unchanged, or hold while the situation closes in. The third assumes a fixed relation between numbers of people and freedom. The fourth measures the rise in the reader's information rather than in the character's options, which can be the opposite of each other.
questions.hint: Ask how many things the character can still do at the start and at the end.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: identify the withdrawal of options across three sentences
questions.stem: A passage runs: "She had a sister in the city who would come at a word. In the first week she wrote. In the second week she did not write, because writing would have meant asking, and asking would have meant admitting she was not managing. In the third week the sister wrote to her, and the letter said they had let the flat go." What changes across these three sentences?

options.text: The option of being helped by the sister, withdrawn in two steps and finally taken away by the sister's own action
The time in the story, since a week is compressed into a fortnight and the compression is the acceleration
options.misconception: counts the spans as acceleration, when a slower sequence can be the more alarming one

options.text: The narrator's sympathy, which moves from the sister to the woman in the third sentence
options.misconception: reads the narrator's sympathy as the rising force, when nothing in the text reports a change of feeling

options.text: The number of letters, which goes from one a week to none and then to one that ends the matter
options.misconception: counts objects rather than options, and misses that the final letter is the one she did not send

questions.explanation: The passage rises by subtraction. At the start she has a sister who would come at a word, and that is an option available to her. In the second sentence she stops writing, and the reason given is that the letter would have had to say what she will not say, so the option has been withdrawn from inside. In the third, the sister writes unprompted, which is the option returning in a form she did not choose, and its content is a decision already taken behind her back, so the option is gone entirely. Three sentences, three reductions, and the pressure comes entirely from what has been closed off. The second option counts the calendar, which is the least of what changes. The third attributes a change of feeling to a narrator who reports none. The fourth counts letters as though they were the point.
questions.hint: Ask at each step which of her available courses is closed.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Climax and the choice it forces
questions.learningObjective: state what a climax is by the choice it compels
questions.stem: What makes a moment a story's climax?

options.text: It forces a choice between two things the character has wanted, so that nothing after it can be a matter of holding on and waiting
It is the loudest scene, since a reader's attention marks the point at which the story is decided
options.misconception: identifies the climax with volume, when a quiet decision can carry more than a shout

options.text: It is the last page before the ending, since that is where the text stops letting the character put things off
options.misconception: locates the climax by position in the book rather than by what the character must do

options.text: It is when the reader first guesses what will happen, since a guess is what gives an event its meaning
options.misconception: makes the climax depend on the reader's guess, which can come at any point in the text

questions.explanation: A climax is defined by compulsion rather than by size, and the test is what the character can no longer postpone. A moment in which a character must choose between two things it has wanted cannot be followed by more deliberation, so the story's outcome is settled there, and everything after is what living with the choice is like rather than whether to make it. This is why a climax can be quiet: a hand taking a key out of a lock is a decision, and a quarrel is not. The second option is the commonest identification and it mistakes loudness for necessity, since a character can shout at length without deciding anything. The third goes by position in the book, which is a fact about pagination. The fourth makes the reader's guessing the cause, and a reader may guess early and be wrong, or guess late and be right.
questions.hint: Ask what the character can no longer postpone after this moment.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: locate the choice a climax forces in an invented passage
questions.stem: A passage runs: "The boat would take one more, and the harbour master said so once and would not say it twice. Vess had the fare in her hand, and the man on the slip had the boat's rope, and there was no third thing to do. She looked at the slip for a while, at the length of it, at the weather, at him, and then she put the money in her pocket and walked back up the road, and it was only at the top that she understood that she had made a decision at all." Where is the choice made?

options.text: At she put the money in her pocket, after a sentence that has just denied that any choice existed
At it was only at the top that she understood, because a decision is not made until the person knows about it
options.misconception: defers the climax to the understanding, when the decision has already been made and cannot be unmade

options.text: At the harbour master said so once, because a rule about repetition makes everything after it a consequence
options.misconception: makes a rule about how often a thing may be asked the climax, which is not a decision

options.text: Nowhere, since the passage reports only what Vess looked at, and looking is not acting
options.misconception: reads a report of looking as an absence of action, ignoring the pocket and the road

questions.explanation: The climax is the pocket, because that is where the passage stops offering alternatives. The sentence before it says there was no third thing to do, which means the two courses have been available all along and one of them is now taken; everything after that is walking up a road, and the last clause admits the decision was made without being noticed. That gap between choosing and knowing is what makes this a climax rather than a plan, since a character who deliberated properly would not be discovering it on a hill. The second option puts the climax in the understanding, but understanding is reportable afterwards and a decision is not undone by being noticed. The third promotes a condition to a decision. The fourth treats an inventory of looking as the absence of an act, when the act is in the next clause.
questions.hint: Ask which clause is the last point at which she could still have done otherwise.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a resolution from a denouement
questions.stem: How does a resolution differ from a denouement?

options.text: The resolution settles the question the story raised, and the denouement shows what life is like afterwards, including whatever stays unsettled
The resolution is the last event and the denouement is the paragraph that explains the last event
options.misconception: divides the pair by order of presentation, which is a matter of sequence and not of function

options.text: The resolution is what the narrator feels and the denouement is what the other characters do about it
options.misconception: splits the pair by whose feelings get reported, which is not the distinction the terms make

options.text: They are the same event at two lengths, since a story that resolves is a story that has finished
options.misconception: collapses the pair and so loses the difference between a settled question and a continuing life

questions.explanation: The two terms answer different questions, and the difference is what each one is for. A resolution is the text's answer to the problem it set itself, and it can be an answer, a refusal, or a partial one, but something has to be settled or explicitly left unsettled for the story to be finished. A denouement is the untangling that follows: the household rearranges itself, the remaining people go on, the consequences arrive late, and some threads are shown still open. A novel can have a powerful denouement and no resolution at all, which is what makes an ending feel like an evasion rather than a close. The second option divides them by position in the book, the third by whose feelings are reported, and the fourth treats them as one thing, which removes the only reason for having two words.
questions.hint: Ask which question each one answers.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: state what makes an ending ambiguous rather than merely unfinished
questions.stem: A novel's last page admits two readings, each supported by sentences earlier in the book. What makes such an ending ambiguous rather than simply unfinished?

options.text: Both readings can be shown from the text, so the ambiguity is in the evidence a reader is given rather than in the writer's having stopped
The reader is left to supply an ending, since a good reader is expected to complete a work rather than receive one
options.misconception: makes the ending a task for the reader's taste, when ambiguity is a property of the evidence

options.text: A fact the reader needed has been withheld, so the uncertainty is a hole in what the text supplied
options.misconception: equates any missing information with a defect, though a withheld fact can be the design

options.text: The text must already have been ambiguous earlier, since an ending cannot introduce doubt of its own accord
options.misconception: requires doubt to be established in advance, which is not a condition of how endings work

questions.explanation: The difference between an ambiguous ending and an unfinished one is whether the text has done the work. An ambiguous ending supports two readings, and a reader who prefers one can point to the sentences that support it and cannot be told they have missed anything. An unfinished ending offers one reading and simply withholds the fact that would confirm it, so a reader who disagrees has nothing to hold. That is why a writer who wants ambiguity has to plant: the evidence has to be there for both sides, and the last page must not settle the question in a way that makes one side unavailable. The second option makes the ending a matter of the reader's willingness. The third calls every gap a hole. The fourth is a rule about technique that no account of endings requires.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader who disagrees can point to in the text.

questions.learningObjective: choose the better-supported reading of an ambiguous ending
questions.stem: An invented novel's last line is: "and in the morning the house was as he had left it, and the door was shut, and the key was on the step." Which reading does the sentence's wording best support?

options.text: That he went away and left the key, since the key is the one thing the house does not match and as he had left it measures the house against him
That he came back and locked up after himself, since a shut door in a house like this is usually a locked one
options.misconception: reads the absence of the word locked as though the ordinary inference were the evidence

options.text: That somebody else left the key, since the narrator never says that he went out at all
options.misconception: invents an agent to explain an object, when the sentence names only him

options.text: That nothing at all happened in the night, since the house is described as unchanged
options.misconception: takes an unchanged house as proof that no event occurred

questions.explanation: The wording gives one reading more support than the others, and the support comes from the phrase as he had left it. That phrase sets the house against his last act of leaving, and the sentence then reports three facts: the house matches, the door is shut, and the key is on the step. If the first two are what he left, then the third is the discrepancy, and a key on a step is what a person leaves when they have gone away, or when they have decided not to come back. The second option substitutes a general inference about doors for the evidence of this sentence, and the fourth contradicts the key. The third supplies an agent the sentence does not mention, which is the standard way an ambiguous ending gets over-read.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three reported facts does not match the phrase that precedes it.

questions.topic: A first line that establishes voice
questions.learningObjective: state what a first line of a novel is doing
questions.stem: What is a novel's first line for?

options.text: Its diction and its address, which tell the reader what kind of telling this is and set a promise the rest of the book is read against
Introducing the main character by name, since a reader needs to know who before anything else
options.misconception: assumes a first line must supply names, which a great many first lines do not

options.text: Stating the period, since a reader cannot follow a book that has not told it when it is set
options.misconception: makes historical placement the first duty, which is frequently given later or never

options.text: Saying the most memorable thing in the book, since first lines are the lines that get quoted
options.misconception: grounds a first line's importance in later quotation rather than in what it does for the reading

questions.explanation: A first line establishes a voice and a contract, and a reader spends the rest of the book checking the book against it. If the line is in the first person and self-blaming, then the reader will read every subsequent sentence for that kind of self-blame; if it is flat and procedural, then the reader will look for the flatness to be broken. That is why first lines are written with such care and why they can so easily wreck a novel, since a promise the book does not keep reads as a lie rather than as an opening. The second option is a practical priority rather than a formal one, and plenty of first lines name nobody. The third treats setting-up as the work, and the fourth confuses a first line's function with its afterlife in quotation.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader will be looking for in the next thousand pages.

questions.learningObjective: choose the opening that establishes a defended voice
questions.stem: A novel is to be narrated by a man whose family's firm has failed. Two openings are offered. Which better establishes the voice the book needs?

options.text: The first, since it introduces a man, a financial judgement, and the narrator's distance from it in one sentence, so the reader knows the tone at once
The second, since it supplies a date and a firm, so a reader can locate the novel before anything else happens
options.misconception: prefers the line with the locational facts, which is a different kind of information from voice

options.text: The first, because the word penny is concrete, and concrete words make better openings than abstract ones
options.misconception: argues from the concreteness of one word and ignores what the sentence's construction does

options.text: The second, because it states the failure in its first line, and giving the ending away is what a confident book does
options.misconception: mistakes a statement of premise for a statement of ending, which the sentence does not give away

questions.explanation: The first line's work is to fix a voice, and the first of these does that in one sentence while the second gives facts a reader can get from a contents page. That is a voice a whole book can be written in, and the second line's date and firm name commit the book to nothing about who is telling it. The second option mistakes information for voice. The third argues from one word's concreteness and leaves the sentence's structure unnamed. The fourth confuses premise with ending, and a book that gave away its ending would not be described as confident but as empty.
questions.hint: Ask which line tells the reader what kind of telling to expect.

The second, since an inventory of a place prepares the reader for what the narrator will later do with the house
options.misconception: prefers the inventory for its later usefulness, when a first line's work is to establish who is speaking

options.text: The first, because a first-person pronoun in the opening makes the book a memoir, which is what the narration is
options.misconception: infers a book's form from one pronoun, which fixes nothing at all about the whole

options.text: The second, because an objective opening suits a narrator the reader is meant not to trust
options.misconception: assumes distance from the subject signals unreliability, when a partisan voice can be both close and accurate

questions.learningObjective: state what a description of a place reveals about the person describing it
questions.stem: A traveller describes a village. What does the description reveal?

The village, since a description is a record of a place and the record is what the reader receives
options.misconception: takes a description to be transparent, when every selection in it is a choice

options.text: The accuracy of the traveller, since a richer description proves a more reliable observer
options.misconception: equates detail with reliability, which is a measure of attention and not of truth

options.text: The mood the description creates, since mood is a property of the observer's mind and not of the village
options.misconception: names a general effect and stops, without identifying the specific choice that produced it

questions.learningObjective: identify the detail in a description that reports the observer's state
questions.stem: An invented description runs: "The garden had gone over to the bed of nettles by the time he came back, and the path was still there, and so was the gate, and the gate was not locked, and the hens had got into the beds and were scratching about in the beans and did not seem to mind him at all." Which detail reports the observer rather than the garden?

options.text: Did not seem to mind him at all, since the clause supplies the observer's expectation and finds the garden indifferent to it
The bed of nettles, since an over-grown garden is a sign that nobody has been there
options.misconception: reads a fact about the garden's condition as a report on the man who came back

options.text: The repeated and, since a speaker who uses it that often is out of breath and unable to stop
options.misconception: treats a repeated conjunction as a symptom of the speaker, which it does not reliably show

options.text: The word beans, since naming a particular crop shows that the observer farmed it
options.misconception: infers an occupation from one word, which the sentence nowhere supports

questions.explanation: The last clause is the only part of that sentence that is about the man rather than the garden, because it reports what he expected and what he did not get. questions.learningObjective: state what a metaphor adds beyond illustration
questions.stem: A metaphor compares two things. What does it do that an illustration of the same comparison would not?

options.text: It asserts something about both terms, so a reader has to judge whether the comparison holds rather than merely picture it
Nothing that matters, since a metaphor and an illustration carry the same information in different clothes
options.misconception: reduces the figure to a change of clothing, which loses the claim it makes

options.text: It lets the writer avoid the same statement in plain words, which is the whole point of using a figure
options.misconception: makes the figure a code for something already said, which removes its force

options.text: It shows the writer can see the two things as similar, which is a fact about the writer rather than about the case
options.misconception: redirects the figure from the claim it makes to the writer's perceptiveness

questions.learningObjective: explain how a metaphor in an argument carries the argument forward
questions.stem: In an invented debate, Mr. Amery says: "The reform has been a knife, and a knife is a thing you use on something already there, and the country was already there." What is the figure doing?

options.text: It makes the reform an act of division on an existing thing, and the second clause ties that to what the country already had, so the argument runs inside the comparison
It shows a man of plain habits who prefers simple tools to elaborate ones
options.misconception: reads the image as a detail about the speaker's character instead of the claim it carries

options.text: It decorates the speech, since the argument about the country is complete without the comparison
options.misconception: calls the figure ornamental while ignoring that the claim is built inside it

options.text: It muddles the speech, since a knife stands for other things as well as division
options.misconception: treats the other meanings a figure keeps open as a defect in the figure

The second clause then does the argumentative work inside the figure, since a country that was already there is being cut up rather than built, and a speaker who wants the reform disbelieved has a reason to reach for this comparison. questions.learningObjective: distinguish a symbol from a fixed code
questions.stem: A novel has a recurring object that stands for something without any fixed pairing. What is the difference between that and an allegory?

options.text: A symbol's correspondence is felt rather than decoded, so what it stands for is worked out over the text rather than looked up in a scheme
There is no difference, since both are made things standing for other things
options.misconception: collapses the two terms and so removes the only question the terms exist to ask

options.text: The difference is that a symbol must recur at least three times, while an allegory must be complete on its first page
options.misconception: sets numerical conditions on the two, which is not how either term works

options.text: The difference is that a symbol is an object and an allegory is a person, so the two cannot be confused
options.misconception: reduces the distinction to what the symbol happens to be made of

questions.explanation: The distinction is about whether a correspondence is fixed, and an allegory is a scheme in which each thing has its assigned other thing, so that a reader can translate the text and get a second text out. A symbol does not offer that: what it stands for is settled by the accumulation of the text rather than given at the start, so two readers can find different and equally supported meanings in the same object, and a reader who disagrees cannot be told they have decoded it wrongly. That is what makes a symbol harder to write and easier to argue about. The second option is a definition that erases the difference. The third invents counting rules. The fourth is a category error, since the same object can serve in an allegory or as a symbol depending on what the text does with it.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader who disagrees has decoded the object wrongly.

questions.topic: A symbol without a fixed meaning
questions.learningObjective: say why a symbol cannot be given a single translation
questions.stem: In an invented novel, the same white stone is carried at a wedding, at a funeral, and into a quarrel, and after the third it is never mentioned again. Does it have a one-to-one meaning?

options.text: No, since the same object in three scenes can carry luck, grief and accusation at once, and a fixed pairing would have to discard one of them
Yes, since it appears at a wedding and at a funeral, so it stands for marriage and for death
options.misconception: assigns a meaning per scene and then calls the total one-to-one, which is a translation and not a symbol

options.text: No, since the novel never explains the stone, so nothing has been assigned to it in the first place
options.misconception: assumes a meaning requires an author's explanation, which is the opposite of the claim

options.text: Yes, since three appearances are too few for a symbol and the object is a detail of the house
options.misconception: sets a numerical threshold for symbolism, which a form cannot supply

questions.explanation: A one-to-one meaning would require the stone to stand for a single thing, and three scenes that pull it in three directions rule that out. At a wedding it is a wish, at a funeral it is a keepsake, and in the quarrel it is an accusation, and these are not three names for one concept but three uses that the novel does not reconcile. The second option is the translation in disguise, and it is the error of every scheme-based account of a symbol. The third mistakes an unexplained object for an empty one, and the fourth counts appearances, which is a fact about the text's length and not about what the object does.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader must discard in order to give the object one meaning.

questions.learningObjective: state what makes a planted detail a foreshadowing
questions.stem: A novel mentions a locked garden gate in chapter two, passes over it for thirty chapters, and returns to it in the last. What made the first mention a foreshadowing?

That it warned the reader the ending would involve a gate, so the ending was less surprising
options.misconception: treats foreshadowing as a promise about the plot rather than as a preparation for re-reading

options.text: That the narrator omitted any explanation of it, so the reader was given less than the ending later required
options.misconception: reduces the device to withholding, which is not the same as planting

options.text: That it appeared in an early chapter, since anything early can be read afterwards as a preparation
options.misconception: makes the effect a function of position on the page, which any detail could claim

The first mention was a plant because the last chapter is where it was planted for, not because of anything about itself. The third confuses planting with withholding, and the fourth would make any early detail a foreshadowing, which is not a description of anything.

A spoon in a drawer, so that the object left behind is the thing the ending is really about
options.misconception: fixes the payoff on one object and misses that it is the number that recurs

options.text: The disagreement about the number, so that a reader knows the household is already at odds before anything else happens
options.misconception: reads a discrepancy as planted conflict, when the discrepancy is never raised again

options.text: Nothing at all, since the last chapter never refers back to the second in so many words
options.misconception: requires an explicit reference back, when a repeated number in the same order is a reference

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a flat character from a round one
questions.stem: How does a flat character differ from a round one?

A flat character is simple and a round character is complex, which is the only distinction the words support
options.misconception: restates the pair as simple and complex, a judgement about amount rather than about structure

options.text: A flat character is written in few words and a round character in many, so the two differ in the space they are given
options.misconception: confuses the room a character is given in the text with the number of traits the character has

options.text: A flat character changes over the story and a round character does not, which is the reverse of what is usually said
options.misconception: reverses the pair, though change over time is a sign of the round rather than the flat

answer.exemplar: The two devices are aimed at different readers, and the text gets a third one out of the gap between them. A withheld fact creates an expectation: the reader builds something from what has been supplied, and the expectation is itself a kind of partial knowledge, so the reader is committed before the fact arrives. An unreliable narrator makes that commitment dangerous, because the evidence the reader built the expectation on came through a source the text has already shown to be self-serving, and so a reader who trusts the narrator has to abandon the expectation, while a reader who does not trust the narrator cannot be sure what was withheld at all. Put together, the devices produce a reader who is holding two incompatible accounts, one provisional and one distrusted, and that reader is in a position no single device could create. The answer above says which device is aimed at whom, what each does to the reader's commitment, and why the two together require a reader who is neither credulous nor dismissive. A reader who notices only the withholding waits for a fact and reads the ending as a delivery; a reader who notices only the narrator reads the withholding as evidence of evasion and reads the ending as a dodge. Neither of those readings is wrong, and each is incomplete.

questions.explanation: An explanation of two devices has to do three things, and this kind of item fails when it does only the first. It must name what each device does on its own, since each is separately visible and a reader who has only a general sense of both cannot be shown the interaction. It must say who each is aimed at, because a withheld fact and a shifting narrator make different demands, and a text that aimed both at the same reader would produce confusion rather than this double position. And it must state what the reader ends up holding, which is the part the question asks for and the part most explanations skip, since they tend to close on a claim about the author rather than on the reader's situation. The temptation is to say the two devices reinforce each other, which is a description of adjacency and not of a relation.
questions.hint: Ask who each device is aimed at, and what a reader is left holding.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Testing a claim about narrative technique
questions.learningObjective: state what must be established before a claim about a technique is accepted
questions.stem: Before a claim that a text uses a named narrative technique should be accepted, what has to be established?

options.text: That the text's own sentences support the claim, since a technique is a description of what sentences do and not a label attached to them
That the reader has covered the whole text, since a technique can only be judged across a work
options.misconception: makes thoroughness the test, when a claim can be checked against the sentences it names

options.text: That no other technique could produce the same effect, since one effect has one cause
options.misconception: requires exclusive causes, which no reading of a text can establish

options.text: That the effect is the one the author intended, since intention settles what a technique is for
options.misconception: asks for intention, which cannot be checked from the text and is not needed to describe what the text does

questions.explanation: A claim about a technique is a claim about the text's sentences, so it is settled by looking at them. If a reader says the chapter is in one sustained tense, the question is what tense the sentences are in, and if a reader says the narrator is unreliable, the question is which sentence reports something the text elsewhere contradicts. That makes the claim falsifiable, which is the property that separates a reading from a preference. The second option confuses breadth of reading with correctness of description, and a claim can be false in one paragraph. The third asks for exclusive causes, which no text can supply, since two techniques very often do the same work. The fourth asks about intention, which is not checkable and not necessary, since a technique is a description of what is there rather than a report of what was meant.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence in the text the claim is about.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A claim contradicted by one sentence
questions.learningObjective: show a claim about tense failing against a single sentence
questions.stem: A critic writes: "This chapter is narrated throughout in a single sustained present tense, and the tense never breaks." One sentence in the chapter reads: "The ferry had been due for an hour before she got to the quay." What does that sentence do?

options.text: It breaks the claim, since a past perfect marks something completed before another past event, so the chapter is not in a single present throughout
It leaves the claim standing, since one sentence in a past tense cannot establish a chapter's tense
options.misconception: dismisses a counter-example, when the claim was made about every sentence in the chapter

options.text: It shows the chapter is too long to have held one tense throughout, which is a fact about the chapter's length
options.misconception: explains the failure by length, which is a fact about pagination and not about grammar

options.text: It shows the sentence is quoted speech, so the narration's own tense is unaffected by it
options.misconception: assumes the sentence is quoted, which the chapter nowhere marks and which would need saying

questions.explanation: The claim is universal, so one counter-example defeats it, and this sentence is a counter-example. Had been due is a past perfect: it places the ferry's lateness as complete before she arrived, which requires a past time of arrival to be complete before. A present-tense narration can report a completed past state, but it cannot construct a past perfect, which needs two past reference points and so needs a past tense narration to have one. The sentence therefore establishes a second tense in the chapter and the claim fails on it. The second option is the reaction the claim invites, and it works by dropping the universality, since the critic said throughout. The third is about length. The fourth invents a marker of quoted speech, which would have to be in the text.
questions.hint: Ask what two past reference points the sentence's verb requires.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A technique claim weighed against its support
questions.learningObjective: weigh the support given for a claim about narrative technique
questions.stem: A critic claims that an invented chapter is written in free indirect discourse throughout. The support offered is that the chapter contains several sentences with no quotation marks and no tag, and that one of those sentences contains the word obviously, which the chapter's narrator never uses. What is wrong with the support?

options.text: Two things: untagged sentences are also simply reported speech or plain narration, and one word the narrator avoids is a habit of one character, not a feature of a mode
Nothing, since a chapter without quotation marks throughout is in free indirect discourse by definition
options.misconception: concedes the whole argument on a criterion that does not define the mode

options.text: Only the second point, since untagged sentences are indeed the mark of the mode, and the word is the weak part of the case
options.misconception: overturns a sound part of the argument and upholds a criterion that is not sufficient

options.text: That the chapter is too short to establish a mode used throughout, since modes need a length to appear in
options.misconception: argues from the chapter's length, which has no bearing on whether its sentences are marked or unmarked

questions.explanation: Both parts of the support fail, and they fail for the same reason, which is that each identifies a feature that can occur outside the mode. An untagged sentence with no quotation marks may be plain narration in the third person, or a report of somebody's speech without quotes, and those are extremely common, so their presence is not evidence at all. The word obviously is a stronger point and still not enough, because a habit of diction belongs to a voice and a mode belongs to a grammar, and a narrator can avoid a word and a chapter can still be reported speech throughout. The second option states a definition the mode does not have. The third is a compound error, since it defends the untagged criterion and drops the better point. The fourth is about length, which settles nothing here.
questions.hint: Ask whether each piece of evidence could occur in a chapter with no free indirect discourse in it at all.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The best-supported account of a technique
questions.learningObjective: choose the account of a technique best supported by the text
questions.stem: An invented novel's chapter is described in four ways. A: it is written throughout in a single sustained present tense. B: it is narrated throughout in the third person by a narrator who knows what every character is thinking. C: it is limited throughout to one character, so that everything reported has passed through her attention. D: it is narrated in a mixture of the first and second person, which is unusual and deliberate. Which account is best supported by a chapter that runs: "The kitchen was not clean and Maren had not made it so, and she knew what her sister thought about the state of the kitchen, and she had known for some years, and the knowing had stopped being a thing she did to herself and become a thing she merely had."

options.text: C, since every fact the sentence reports is available to Maren and none requires knowledge of anyone else's mind
B, since knowing what everybody thinks is what makes a narrator the centre of a chapter
options.misconception: accepts a claim of total knowledge that the sentence's grammar makes unavailable

options.text: A, since a chapter with no past-tense verb in it is in the present throughout
options.misconception: confuses the absence of one tense with the presence of another, which is a different test

options.text: D, since the sentence's use of she throughout keeps the narration at a distance from the reader
options.misconception: reads a third-person pronoun as a mixture of persons, which it is not

questions.explanation: The sentence reports a kitchen, a state of mind, a belief about what somebody else thinks, and a history, and each of those is available to one person sitting in a kitchen she has not cleaned, so a limit on knowledge is being maintained throughout. The phrase about knowing what her sister thought is the test, because knowing what somebody else thinks is not something a limited narrator can do directly, and here it arrives as Maren's own knowledge, which is a different fact. The second option asserts a total narrator, and a sentence cannot tell the reader what the sister is thinking. The third confuses the absence of a past tense with the presence of a present one, and the chapter plainly reports past events. The fourth calls a consistent third person a mixture of persons.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything reported has to have passed through one person's attention.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: reconstruct the order of a fragmented sequence from what each section requires
questions.stem: A text is printed as four sections out of order. Restore the order. The letter's arrival must come before the fair, because the fair is what the letter is about; the winter must come after the fair, since the letter is read again in it; and the last section is the one in which the letter is burned unopened by somebody else.

options.text: The section in which the letter is burned unopened by somebody else
The section about the winter after the fair, in which the letter is read again
The section in which the letter arrives
The section about the fair that the letter concerns

questions.explanation: Each position is fixed by a condition the text supplies, and no step is a matter of judgement. The arrival must precede the fair, because the letter is about the fair and cannot be about something that has not happened, so the arrival is first and the fair second. The winter follows the fair, since the letter is read again in it, which puts it third. The last condition fixes the remaining section, so the burning of the unopened letter by somebody else is fourth, and the fact that it is somebody else gives the sequence its final note without altering any of the three earlier positions. The order cannot be rearranged, since every pair of adjacent sections is related by a condition rather than by a preference.
questions.hint: Apply each condition and note which section it pins down.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: reconstruct the order of a subplot's stages
questions.stem: Four statements describe the stages through which a subplot passes. Restore the order in which they occur.

options.text: The subplot is introduced as an ordinary errand, with nothing to mark it as a line of action of its own
The subplot's purpose is stated late, and the earlier stages are then read in the light of what it turns out to have been doing
The subplot is repeated at intervals, and the repetition is what the reader notices before the reason for it
The subplot crosses the main plot once, and somebody who belongs to the main plot turns out to be in it

questions.explanation: A subplot has a shape, and the shape is why a reader can be shown its purpose late. It begins by being unremarkable, because a thread that announces itself as a thread will be read as one from the start and will never be able to alter the main plot by surprise. It is then repeated at intervals, and the repetition is what registers before the understanding does, so the reader has a feeling of something recurring that cannot yet be named. It crosses into the main plot once, which is the moment its two accounts turn out to be one set of facts. And its purpose is stated last, so that a reader who has been holding the earlier stages in mind can re-read them, which is the only stage at which the device is complete. Reordering these gives a reader a clue before a thread, or an explanation before the evidence for it.
questions.hint: Ask which stage lets a reader re-read the earlier ones.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The order a narrator discloses facts
questions.learningObjective: reconstruct the order in which a narrator reveals a chain of facts
questions.stem: A narrator discloses four facts: A, that the sale did not happen; B, that the house had been empty for two years; C, that a man came in October to measure it; D, that he left the key in the door. The text's first sentence gives A, its last sentence gives D, and B is given after the visit that it explains. Restore the order of disclosure.

options.text: That the sale did not happen, which the text's first sentence gives
That he left the key in the door, which the text's last sentence gives
That a man came in October to measure it
That the house had been empty for two years, which the text gives after the visit it explains

questions.explanation: Two of the four positions are fixed outright and the remaining two follow from a single stated relation. The stem gives A as the first sentence and D as the last, so the sale's failure opens the account and the key closes it, which is also the shape of a chapter that has decided to report only what is recorded. Between them sit the visit and the emptiness. Since B is given after the visit it explains, the emptiness of the house is something the visit discovers, and so the visit comes third and the emptiness fourth. The order therefore runs the failure, the visit, the emptiness, the key, and no step is left to preference: reversing the middle two would place an explanation before the thing that called for it.
questions.hint: Note the two fixed positions, then place the rest by the stated relation.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: explain what a shift in focalisation does inside a scene
questions.stem: An invented novel holds a scene to one character for six pages and then, for half a page, moves to a different character in the same room. Explain what that half page can do that six pages could not, and why the shift can carry more than a flashback would.

answer.exemplar: The half page is not a change in what happens but in what the reader is entitled to know, and that is the whole of its power. Six pages locked to the first character have taught the reader that everything in the room arrived through that person's attention, so any fact in it has been read as that person's estimate. A half page in the second character breaks the guarantee without breaking the scene: the reader is now in the same room from a different pair of senses, and a thing that was one person's guess a moment ago can turn out to be a fact. That is a revelation delivered by a change of vantage rather than by new events, which is why it costs no time and why it lands harder than an explanation would. It is more economical than a flashback because it does not leave the scene, and it is more disruptive because a flashback is a request to wait while a shift is a demand to re-read the last six pages, which the reader will do at once. The answer above specifies what the six pages taught, what the half page revises, and why the shorter unit does the more work, since an explanation that is longer and later would arrive after the reader had settled.

questions.explanation: An explanation of a shift in focalisation has to distinguish what changes from what does not, because the temptation is to describe it as a change in events and the whole effect depends on there being none. It must also say what the reader has been taught before the shift, since the guarantee of a single vantage is what makes the shift informative. And it should say why the technique is economical, which is the comparison the question asks for and the part most answers omit. The failure mode here is an explanation that is all enthusiasm, or one that says the shift shows what the character really feels without asking how the reader can be given a fact that the previous character could not see. The question asks what the half page can do, and the answer has to name a specific thing about the reader's standing rather than the general effect of variety.
questions.hint: Ask what the six pages taught the reader, and what the half page revises.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An ambiguous ending with an unreliable narrator
questions.learningObjective: explain how an ambiguous ending and an unreliable narrator work together
questions.stem: An invented novel's last chapter is narrated by a woman whose unreliability the text has established, and the chapter's final sentence admits two readings. Explain how the two devices work together, and what the ending gives a reader who has tracked both.

answer.exemplar: The ending and the narrator are solving two different problems, and the reader who has tracked both is reading a third thing that neither produces alone. An ambiguous ending asks the reader to hold two readings without preferring either, and that demand is usually met by planting evidence for each. A narrator whose unreliability is established means the evidence for both readings is evidence she chose to lay down, so the choice itself becomes a fact: she put the sentence about the key where a reader would see it, and she put the sentence about the shutter where a reader would see it, and she left them unreconciled. The ending is therefore not only two possible meanings but a report of a mind arranging to leave two, which is a more disturbing object than either meaning alone, because the refusal is a decision rather than a gap. A reader who has tracked both is holding a moral and a formal fact at once: she could have closed either account and did not. A reader who has noticed only the ambiguity is asking which of two things happened; a reader who has noticed only the narrator is asking whether anything in the chapter should be believed, and neither question gets to the ending's actual content.

questions.explanation: An explanation of two devices working together has to keep three things apart, and the commonest failure is to describe them separately and then assert that they reinforce each other, which is adjacency and not a relation. It must say what each device does alone, since the ambiguous ending distributes evidence and the unreliable narrator makes that evidence a choice. It must say what the combination produces, which here is a decision rather than a gap, and that is a different object from either device on its own. And it must say what the reader who tracks both has, since the question asks for that specifically and an answer that ends on a general claim about the novel will have missed it. An explanation that praises the book or explains what unreliable narrators are in general does none of the three.
questions.hint: Ask what the narrator chose to leave unreconciled.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: explain what a subplot does to a reader's understanding of a main plot
questions.stem: An invented novel runs a short thread about a woman who buys a ticket every Thursday for two hundred pages, and at the end it turns out she has been keeping an address in use so that a man can neither settle his father's affairs nor sell a house. Explain what the subplot does, and why its length is part of the design rather than a fault.

answer.exemplar: The subplot does one job and does it late, and the length is what makes the job possible. For most of the novel the ticket is an errand: a woman on a platform, a week that is a week, a small expense that no character remarks on twice. That ordinariness is the device's work, because a thread that announced itself as a thread would be read as a thread from the first page and could never afterwards alter the main plot by surprise. So the length is not padding but duration, and two hundred pages is the time it takes for a reader to stop seeing a woman and start seeing an address. When the link is made, the effect is on the other account rather than on this one: the man's long obstruction, his lawyers, his letters to a house that would not sell, are now all consequences of a woman buying a ticket, and a reader has to re-read the whole of the first plot as a series of effects rather than failures of nerve. The explanation above says why the thread must look ordinary, what the length buys, and what the reader must revise afterwards, because an account that only noted the subplot was a clue would describe its content and not its structure.

questions.explanation: An explanation of a subplot has to establish that it alters the main plot rather than accompanying it, and it has to do that with the reader's own re-reading in view rather than in general terms. The second thing it must do is account for the length, which is the question's own difficulty and the point at which most answers complain about the two hundred pages instead of explaining them. The third is to name the specific thing the reader must revise, since a subplot that changed nothing could not be described as altering the first plot at all. A weak answer will say the subplot adds depth or interest, which is a judgement about the book and not a description of the device, or it will say the subplot was really the main plot all along, which is a reversal of emphasis and not an account of what the threads did to each other.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader has to re-read afterwards, and what the length was for.
